Excellency.

Mr. President, Excellencies, I thank the French Presidency for convening this important debate. For nearly 10 years, I have seen what peacekeepers can do, what they can do when the Security Council stands behind them, and what they endure when it is divided. We do not lack tools. What we lack all too often is the political space to use them. And that is the starting point of the review of peace operations requested in the Pact for the Future. Excellencies, peacekeeping is above all a political instrument. It is deployed to support political solutions, never as a substitute for them. For three decades, We sent peacekeepers mainly to help the parties to a civil war implement a comprehensive peace agreement. And today, such agreements are rarer than at any time in decades. They are harder to reach and more fragile. Most of our missions now operate where peace remains elusive. They are asked to contain the damages of war that the parties feel little pressure to end and that outside actors sometimes feed. The ground has shifted. Too often, our mandates have not. Peacekeepers are attacked. Civilians are targeted. International law is violated with a mounting sense of impunity. Drones. Lethal autonomous weapons, disinformation amplified by artificial intelligence. The very nature of conflict is changing fast. Meanwhile, peacekeeping budgets have been slashed and the number of troops and police are greatly reduced. Continuous improvement matters, and we're doing so from Action for Peacekeeping to the UN80 Initiative. But that can only take us so far. The success of every mission requires your unity and a recognition of the evolving context in which we operate. And that is why the review calls for a reset. Allow me to reflect on five overreaching priorities. First, put peacemaking first. Let me be clear, peacekeeping operations should be deployed only when a peace agreement, or at least a robust ceasefire, is in place. Peacekeepers can do a lot to preserve the peace, but we cannot keep peace where there is no peace to keep. The way back to peacekeeping runs through peacemaking, and the Charter gives us Council the tools including Chapter VI. I urge you to use them to investigate disputes before they become wars, to visit the countries concerned, to build a shared understanding of the facts, which is the foundation of shared action, We will make fuller use of our good offices and the work of our missions and envoys, as we have done in Colombia and as we are doing in Cyprus. Not every crisis requires a new mission, but every crisis requires a political strategy and the coherent support of Member States. Second, forge a new partnership with host States. Peace cannot be imported. It must be built from within by the national actors who hold the key. That means consulting host states at the mandating stage and at every renewal, while also hearing all other parties to the conflict and civil society. It means an open, continuing conversation with the countries that contribute troops and police. And it could mean, for each peacekeeping mandate, a political mechanism, such as a compact between this Council, the Secretariat, and the host state, with each of us committing to what the others need, adherence and support to the mandate of the mission, on the forces and the equipment it requires, and on the technologies it must be allowed to use. Third, mandate for the world as it is. And that means agreeing before peacekeepers deploy on a longer-term vision on what they are meant to help achieve and, when appropriate, shorter-term objectives to measure progress. Mandates must be focused on what peacekeeping missions do best, particularly politics and security, and where mandated the protection of civilians. Protection built into missions mandate from the outset and how they are planned, mandated and resourced so that when civilians are threatened, peacekeepers can act decisively. And an exit strategy planned from the start of any mission. It means treating every renewal as a strategic opportunity to adapt. And when circumstances change, mandates must evolve. The Secretariat will provide frank assessments on what is working and what is not, and propose what to change, when to reconfigure, and when to leave.

Force empower the operations this Council mandates. Agility is not in the Secretariat's hands alone. Missions cannot move at the speed of events when they are bound by rigid budgetary rules and administrative procedures. Efficiency means making every dollar count. But it can never replace our shared duty to fund peacekeeping predictably and adequately. Readiness means investing steadily in the people and tools of peacekeeping, including more mobile missions, the military and police capabilities of tomorrow, and the means to counter drones. Yet in several places, peacekeepers are still denied technology that any modern force would consider basic. That undermines their ability to fulfill their mandates. Overcoming those restrictions will take the active support of this Council. Readiness also requires a skilled, diverse workforce with the full, equal and meaningful participation of women at all levels. And it requires accountability in both directions, for the conduct of our personnel and for attacks on those who serve. Every day, in some of the most dangerous places on earth, peacekeepers create space for dialogue and open pathways to peace. They do so at great risk, And too many have paid the highest price. I honor their courage and the memory of those who never come home. Resolution 2823, which this Council adopted unanimously, must now be implemented. No impunity, no exceptions. Fifth, work as a network. No organization can address today's conflicts alone. Peacekeepers are part of a wider system: United Nations entities, regional organizations, and the host country, each with its own strengths. Where UN agencies, funds, and programs can deliver better on a task, they should do it and receive the funds to do so, so that peacekeepers can concentrate on what only they can do. And when they leave, the gains do not leave with them. Our regional partners, above all the African Union, have also an essential role. With resolution 2719, this Council made a landmark commitment to predictable financing for African Union-led peace support operations. It's time to bring it to life, case by case, always in the service of political solutions. UN peacekeeping operations should only be deployed when there is a peace agreement or a robust ceasefire. When circumstances require, we need peace enforcing, not peacekeeping. When peace enforcing is justified, it can be led by regional forces or coalitions, as this Council decided in the case of Haiti, with United Nations logistical support. But force must serve a political strategy, never replace one. It must respect the Charter and adhere to international law. And it must answer to this Council. Without those safeguards, the use of force risks deepening the very conflicts it is meant to end. The Secretariat should play a strong role in ensuring those safeguards, providing the necessary technical support, and ensuring that enforcement action is rooted in an inclusive political strategy. And where peacekeepers serve alongside enforcement operations, there must be no doubt about who does what, and who answers for it. Excellencies, unity is built through effort, engagement, and compromise. That is, first and foremost, the work of this Council. No mandate, no budget, no technology can replace it. But you are not alone. The Secretariat has a fundamental responsibility to actively support you and the Review holds us to it. In the shadow of war, people still look to the blue helmets and trust them. Let us be worthy of that trust every day. Let us invest in peace. Let us be accountable and modernize ourselves, being more effective and cost-effective. Let's stand united behind those who keep it and forge together new pathways to peace. Thank you.

I thank the Secretary-General for his briefing and the report, which is at the heart of the United Nations Action and Security Council's as well. I now give the floor to Dear members of the Council, I give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Javier Martinez Acha Vasquez, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Panama.

Good afternoon, Secretary-General, Excellencies, Ambassadors. Allow me to begin by thanking the French Presidency for convening this debate. and the Secretary-General for the report that invites us today to reflect on the future of United Nations peace operations. We also are grateful for the work of the Department of Peace Operations and the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, whose efforts continue to be indispensable to the fulfilment of the mandate entrusted to us by the Charter. This review responds to a decision taken by Member States in the Pact for the Future to adapt the tools of the United Nations to the realities of present and future conflicts, enabling responses that are more agile, flexible and tailored to each situation. But Panama believes that this review requires us to do more than simply asking how our peace operations should change. We must first ask what purpose they serve. What is the purpose of the United Nations when it decides to act in the face of conflict? For Panama, the answer is clear. The United Nations is not called upon merely to manage conflicts. It is called upon to open pathways towards overcoming them. Mr. President, peace operations have meaning when they preserve and when they expand the political space needed to achieve a peaceful and sustainable solution. When they protect the civilian population, when they build trust, when they help to keep channels of dialogue open, when they strengthen national institutions, and when they create the conditions for peace to be sustained after the United Nations presence has ended, because peace cannot depend indefinitely on an international mission. The success of a peace operation is measured not by how long a mission remains in place, but by how long peace can endure after the mission has withdrawn. This is what our horizon must be. Mr. President, the experience of Sierra Leone demonstrates that this horizon is attainable. The United Nations accompanied the country through various stages of its recovery, from peacekeeping to institutional consolidation. And There is one particularly powerful image from that experience. Years after the closure of UNAMSIL, Sierra Leone had not only strengthened its democratic institutions, but it had become a troop contributing country to United Nations peace operations. That is one of the clearest examples of what a successful transition means. A country that once received international solidarity ultimately becomes part of that international solidarity. Mr. President, the experience of the Democratic Republic of the Congo reminds us, in turn, that the protection of civilians remains a central responsibility of the United Nations, and that peace operations must be integrated into a broader political strategy. No mission can, by itself, address the root causes of a conflict. It can contain violence. It can protect lives. It can open space. It can provide support. But there is a boundary that we must clearly recognize, namely, force can contain violence, but it is politics is what can bring it to an end. This is why the political role of the United Nations is irreplaceable. the good offices of the Secretary-General, preventive diplomacy, mediation, political dialogue, confidence building. These remain amongst the most powerful tools available to our Organization to prevent a crisis from reaching the point of no return. Investing in them is not an alternative to peace operations. It is an investment in reducing the length of time for which peace operations are needed. Mr. President, the strategic environment has changed profoundly. Conflicts are more protracted. They involve more actors. The lines between internal and international conflicts are increasingly complex. Technology is transforming the nature of warfare. Information and disinformation can accelerate crises, and geopolitical rivalries are increasingly being projected onto local settings. Faced with this reality, the United Nations cannot respond simply by doing the same things with new tools. The world has changed. Our way of making peace must also change. And this brings us to a second reflection. For decades now, we have spoken of exit strategies. Well, the time has come to also speak of entry strategies. Before deploying a mission, we must know what political opportunity we are seeking to protect. What problem are we seeking to resolve? What change are we seeking to make possible? What conditions must exist for the mission to have a genuine prospect for success? And above all, how do we want it to end? A mission should not begin by asking how many resources it needs. It should begin by asking what political change it seeks to make possible. Mr. President, The quality of a peace operation begins before it arrives on the ground. It begins with the quality of its mandate, clear mandates, achievable objectives, defined priorities, sufficient resources, a coherent political strategy, and a viable transition. When that vision exists from the outset, subsequent decisions become more coherent. Strategic reviews cease to be administrative exercises. Mandate renewals become genuine opportunities to ask ourselves what is working, what needs to change, and whether the mission continues to respond to the reality on the ground. For that reason, my country believes that peace operations should be assessed not only by their activities, but also by their political impact. Have they helped to reduce violence? Have they protected civilians? Have they built trust? Have they created space for negotiation? Have they strengthened national institutions? Have they enabled societies themselves progressively to assume responsibility for their own peace? A peace operation should not be judged solely by what it does while it is present, but by what it leaves behind when it withdraws. Mr. President, nor can the future of peace operations be built around a single formula. Not all conflicts require the same response. Not all require blue helmets. Some require mediation. Others require a political presence. Others the protection of civilians. Others institutional support. Others electoral assistance, strengthening the rule of law, or peace-building. Many require a combination of these tools. For that reason, Panama supports a genuinely flexible vision of the peace operations system. The future does not necessarily require larger missions. It requires missions that are better suited to their purpose. We need responses tailored to each conflict, not a one-size-fits-all approach, but the right tool for each opportunity for peace. And that flexibility must also extend to our technological capabilities. New technologies can improve early warning, the protection of civilians, ceasefire monitoring, and the safety and security of our personnel. But we must remember an essential truth: artificial intelligence can help us anticipate risks. It cannot replace political intelligence. Technology can provide information. The decision to make peace remains a human one. Mr. President, no mission can sustain a peace process on its own. The greatest strength of the United Nations lies precisely in its ability to integrate efforts. The Security Council, the General Assembly, the Peacebuilding Commission, the agencies, funds and programs. regional and sub-regional organizations, civil society, academia, the private sector, and above all, the states themselves and the societies directly affected. The challenge is to bring different capabilities to bear in pursuit of the same political objective, because a peace mission should not become an island within the United Nations system. It must form part of an architecture for peace. Mr. President, we must also be realistic about resources. The organization's current liquidity crisis is seriously constraining our collective ability to implement the mandates entrusted by this Council. Rapid reductions in personnel and capacities were not accompanied by proper transition planning. can create vacuums that are ultimately exploited by those seeking to deepen instability. Panama, therefore, reiterates its call on all Member States to fulfill their financial obligations fully and on time. We cannot ask our missions to do more while providing them with fewer means to carry out what this Council has entrusted to them. A mandate without resources is not a promise, it is a vulnerability. Mr. President, the protection of those who protect peace must also occupy a central place in this review. Panama welcomes the unanimous adoption of resolution 2823, which strengthens accountability for crimes committed against peacekeeping personnel. The resolution was adopted by all 15 members of the Council and received the support of more than 150 States during the negotiating process. Those who risk their lives under the United Nations flag cannot be allowed to become victims of impunity. Protecting civilians is a mandate. Protecting those who protect them must also be one. Mr. President, wars rarely end simply because the fighting stops. A ceasefire can silence the guns, but peace begins when the parties find a reason not to take them up again. A blue helmet can protect a space for dialogue, but no blue helmet can substitute for dialogue. This is why we must identify political opportunities when they arise, because those opportunities are fragile. Sometimes they last for months, at times only a few days. The responsibility of the United Nations is to recognize them in time and mobilize the full potential of the multilateral system to strengthen them before they disappear. The peace process in Colombia is an example of how a political opportunity accompanied by the will of the parties and the support of the international community can open the way towards a negotiated solution. It reminds us of something fundamental. Peace cannot be imposed from outside. It is built when there is political will within and when the international community knows how to support it. Mr. President, Panama believes that this review should lead us to a conclusion that is simple yet profound. We do not merely need better peace operations. We need a better architecture for preventing conflict, mediating, protecting, peacebuilding and sustaining peace. We need more agile operations, clearer mandates, better tailored responses, greater integration between political and operational tools, better planned transitions, greater cooperation with regional organizations, predictable resources, and above all, a renewed primacy of politics. Because the ultimate objective of a peace operation is not to remain, it is to make its own departure possible. And perhaps that is the most noble paradox of peace operations. A mission achieves its true success when the day comes that it is no longer needed. Mr. President, 80 years ago, the Charter of the United Nations entrusted us with a historic responsibility to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war. Today, we cannot abandon that purpose, nor can we fulfill it with tools designed for a world that no longer exists. We must adapt our operations to the conflicts of our time, without losing sight of the principles on which this organization was founded. We must make use of technology without forgetting politics. We must strengthen capacities without losing sight of purpose. We must deploy when necessary, but we must also prevent before it is too late. And we must know not only when to enter, but also when and how to leave. Because ultimately, we must not manage conflicts indefinitely. We must create the conditions for overcoming them. Ladies and gentlemen, allow me to conclude by recalling the words of former Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjold: "The pursuit of peace and progress cannot end in a few years in either victory or defeat. The pursuit of peace and progress, with its trials and errors, its successes and its setbacks, can never be relaxed and never abandoned." May that pursuit continue to guide the United Nations, and may our peace operations continue to serve not only as instruments for containing violence, but as bridges towards a peace capable of sustaining itself, because the true measure of a peace operation is not how long the United Nations flag remains, it is how long peace remains after that flag has been withdrawn. Thank you very much.
I thank His Excellency Mr. Javier Martinez-Acha Vazquez, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Panama. I now give the floor to Pakistan.

Thank you, President. We would like to thank the French presidency for convening this debate. And let me also welcome the participation of the distinguished foreign minister of Panama, and we thank him for his comprehensive statement. President, allow me to also thank the Secretary-General for his briefing and his report on the review of the future of United Nations peace operations. This discussion comes at a critical moment, offering Member States an opportunity to reflect on the SG's recommendations and on how UN peacekeeping should evolve to remain relevant, strong, effective and fit for purpose in a changing environment. President Pakistan brings to this debate the perspective of both a major troop contributing country and as a host state. For over six decades, Pakistan has remained amongst the largest troop contributors to UN peacekeeping. With more than 170,000 Pakistani blue helmets having served the UN, and 183 of our peacekeepers having made the ultimate sacrifice in the cause of peace. And Pakistan is also host to United Nations Military Observer Group in India and Pakistan, UNMOGIP, that is mandated to observe the ceasefire in Jammu and Kashmir. And we have also contributed over the years to peacekeeping policy debate with the objective of adapting and strengthening UN peacekeeping. Just to briefly recall, in 2004, that's more than 20 years ago, under Pakistan's presidency of the Security Council at that time, a presidential statement of the council was adopted Number 16, which for the first time in the context of the debate around peacekeeping, referred to and addressed the challenge that was at that time about the surge in demand in peacekeeping, and also introduced to Council's discussion the concept of robust mandates. and rules of engagement for deploying missions with sufficient deterrence, even in risky situations. And then about 10 years later, in January 2013, in another presidency of Pakistan Security Council, the council unanimously adopted Resolution 2086 which was a standalone for the first time, a dedicated resolution of the Security Council on peacekeeping, and it dealt with multi-dimensional peacekeeping. That provide a big momentum to the secretariat's efforts to effectively deploy multi-dimensional peacekeeping missions. Skip 10 years later, We last year in July with support of council members, we adopted resolution 2788 on peaceful settlement of disputes. And this is something that the distinguished minister was highlighting. The need for mediation for good offices and advancing political processes, which are very important. And then in June, together with Denmark, Resolution 2823 on accountability for attacks against peacekeeping. So this experience gives us a practical appreciation of what peacekeeping requires. Political support, credible mandates, sustainable resources, adequate capabilities, host state cooperation, and sustained commitment from the wider membership. President, today peacekeeping is actually under real pressure. No new mission has been established since 2014. Several have closed or drawn down, while political and financial constraints have intensified. However, This should not be misread as a decline of support for peacekeeping. Since 1960s, peacekeeping has moved in cycles of expansion and retrenchment. And the present moment can be seen as another period of realignment. Peacekeeping adapts because conflict changes and because international politics evolve. There is much to unpack. on this subject. However, allow me to limit myself to four key points. First, peacekeeping needs both political backing and a political strategy. The Council must provide clear direction, sustained political support, and adequate resources. Host state consent must also translate into practical cooperation, including freedom of movement, access and support for mandate implementation. At the same time, the primacy of politics must be understood in its proper context. Peacekeeping cannot substitute for political processes, but neither should the principle of primacy of politics become an argument for inaction. In fact, The pursuit of political solutions and peacekeeping should not be mutually exclusive. Even when political processes stall, peacekeeping can contain violence, protect civilians, preserve ceasefires, and create space for politics to resume. We must therefore use this key instrument to create and maintain that space. Second, focused mandates must mean better peacekeeping, not less peacekeeping. A focused mandate is not necessarily a smaller one. It is one that aligns political objectives, tasks, capabilities and resources. One situation may require a light observer mission. light observer presence. Another scenario may entail substantial mobility, aviation, engineering, medical, and protection of civilian capabilities. There is obviously, therefore, no one-size-fits-all model. The sequence should be clear. Define the political objective, design the mandate, identify the capabilities required, and Finally, resource it accordingly. We must not start with a financial ceiling and then shrink the mission to fit it, irrespective of political objectives. Let us also recall that in the context of UN, peacekeeping is a proven cost-effective tool. We should reduce duplications, yes, streamline processes, and use technology better. and enhance partnerships with regional organizations. But efficiency and complementarity should strengthen delivery, not hollow out missions. Third, we must prepare today for the capabilities peacekeeping will need tomorrow. We therefore welcome the SG's reviews proposal for a study of the key police and military capabilities required for future peace operations. Practical, forward-looking and undertaken in close consultation with TCCs and PCCs. This study should inform future force generation training and pledges requirements. Lastly, We must preserve peacekeeping as a genuinely collective UN instrument. Pakistan and Denmark, as Council's peacekeeping duo, with the support of all Council members and the wider membership, have sought to sustain attention to this important instrument in the Council. Resolution 2823 on accountability for crimes against peacekeepers adopted unanimously and co-sponsored by a record 153 member states demonstrated the breadth of support for UN peacekeeping among the wider membership. Similarly, this year's C34 report was adopted by consensus. At a time when we often speak of declining confidence in multilateralism, the wider membership has demonstrated its continuing interest in and commitment to peacekeeping. That collective ownership is one of peacekeeping's greatest strengths. It is therefore incumbent upon this Council to preserve its relevance, credibility, and capacity, and when circumstances require, to take decision and use it, this tool, peacekeeping. President, this is a period of challenge. challenges and realignment. The reset proposed by the SG is necessary, but in resetting peacekeeping, we should be careful not to dismantle the very strengths we may need again tomorrow. We should modernize this instrument while preserving what makes it uniquely United Nations endeavor, its universal legitimacy, Its ability to draw personnel and capabilities from across the membership. Its integrated structures. Its sustainable financing mechanisms. Its institutional knowledge. And the men and women willing to serve under the UN flag with pride, commitment, and honor. That should guide the future of United Nations peacekeeping. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Pakistan for his statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Denmark.

Thank you to the French Presidency for convening this debate. And let me also thank the Secretary-General for his briefing and recommendations, and of course for the review report we received last month. And I welcome His Excellency the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Panama to the Council. Colleagues, peacekeeping is, at its heart, not about mandate, missions, measures or benchmarks. It's also about people. It's about the brave women and men who serve under the UN flag at extraordinary personal risk to protect lives and support peace. And it's about the civilians whose safety and dignity are the very reason the blue helmets are mandated by this Council. It is also with this conviction that Denmark has, together with Pakistan, sought to keep UN peace operations high on the Council's agenda during our Council terms, to recognize their strengths, to address their shortcomings, and to make them fit for the future. Mr. President, the fact that no new UN peacekeeping operation has been mandated since 2014 should not be mistaken for a decline in relevance. UN peacekeeping remains essential to maintain international peace and security. What has declined, and what should be revitalized, is this Council's political will to deploy them, adopt them, and rethink them. Secretary-General, Denmark welcomes your call for a reset. But a reset should not mean a retreat. It should mean ensuring that the UN has the best tools, political strategies, and partnerships to act. And to this end, I would also like to focus on four key points. First, peacekeeping must remain firmly anchored in political strategy with a clear end state. It should create and preserve the conditions for inclusive political solutions, protect civilians, and support peace processes. It is an endeavor encompassing this Council, but also the Secretary-General and the Secretariat. In the Council, we must establish clear, achievable mandates and provide the political backing necessary for peace operations to implement them. We should not simply reproduce existing texts. Every renewal should offer an opportunity to assess objectives, capabilities, and the political strategy, and where necessary, realign them with realities on the ground. From the Secretariat, we need comprehensive planning across components and all levels, frank analysis and early warnings, including when existing mandates or configurations are no longer viable. We need to assess and act on risks rather than avoid difficult conversations. We welcome the suggestions for enhanced use of fact-finding missions, good offices and mediation. The Secretary-General can play an important role in leveraging these tools. Second, Mr. President, mandates must better reflect the realities on the ground. Conflicts are becoming increasingly regional, particularly in Africa. We should strengthen the capacity of missions to address regional conflict dynamics and make better use of regional offices, envoys, and partnerships with regional organizations. However, regionalization should not mean outsourcing responsibility. The UN's universal legitimacy and its unique ability to mobilize and deploy multinational capacities remain a major comparative advantage. Third, effective peacekeeping requires effective and honest relationship with those most concerned. This includes genuine dialogue with host countries and parties to a conflict, meaningful engagement with troop and police contributing countries, and stronger cooperation with regional actors and the wider UN system. National ownership is essential, but so is host state compliance with the obligations that underpin a mission's mandate. Restrictions on the freedom of movement of UN peacekeepers are unacceptable. We must also ensure that attacks against peacekeepers are not met with impunity, as clearly reconfirmed in resolution 2823, and thank you for highlighting that, Mr. Secretary-General. A resolution co-led by Denmark and Pakistan and adopted unanimously in this Council with a record number of co-sponsorship, as the Permanent Representative of Pakistan just mentioned. Perpetrators of crimes against peacekeepers must be held accountable. Fourth, we must be realistic about resources. Denmark fully supports greater efficiency, accountability and cost-effectiveness. But efficiency cannot become a justification for hollowing out missions to the point where they can no longer deliver on their political objectives. Mr. President, in closing, the challenge before us is not to preserve peacekeeping as it was, nor to replace it with new models for their own sake. It is to ensure that when the Security Council chooses to act, the United Nations has the mandate, the capabilities, and the resources to make the actions count. This is the essence of a genuine reset, not a lower ambition for UN peacekeeping, but a better targeted and more politically effective ambition, with people always at its core. Denmark remains fully engaged to make that ambition a reality. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Denmark for her statement. I now give the floor to the representative of the United Kingdom.

Thank you to the Secretary-General for his briefing. At the outset, I pay tribute to the blue helmets who work every day to protect international peace and security. We also honour those who have made the ultimate sacrifice in that service. The safety and security of peacekeepers is essential, and we welcome the unanimous adoption of Security Council Resolution 2823 earlier this year to strengthen accountability for attacks against personnel serving in UN peacekeeping operations. President, we welcome the publication of the Secretary-General's review of the future of all forms of UN peacekeeping operations. Peace operations remain one of the United Nations' most effective tools for maintaining international peace and security. But in the world in which they operate is changing rapidly. Conflicts are becoming more complex, more internationalized, and increasingly shaped by new technologies. Peacekeeping operations must continue to adapt if they are to remain effective. Let me make three points on the primacy of politics, on building more focused, adaptable, and high-performing missions, and on ensuring missions have the tools they need to succeed. First, we welcome the review's emphasis on the primacy of politics. Peacekeeping operations work best where they support a clear political strategy, realistic objectives and a credible path to peace. Missions should be designed with credible exit strategies from the outset, but they must also be able to adapt as circumstances evolve. helping to ensure that when a mission departs, it leaves behind the conditions for a durable peace. Second, we support the review's emphasis on building more focused, adaptable, and high-performing peace operations. Peacekeeping operations should focus on the tasks that they are uniquely placed to deliver, particularly in the political and security spheres, while avoiding duplication elsewhere in the UN system. Mandates should be prioritised and there should be stronger alignment between mandates, resources and political objectives. Performance remains central to mission success. That means ensuring both uniformed and civilian personnel are properly trained, well equipped and accountable for delivery. It also requires maintaining the highest standards of conduct, including a zero tolerance approach to sexual exploitation and abuse. Women's participation is also essential to mission effectiveness. But this is not simply a matter of representation. It improves operational performance, it strengthens engagement with communities, and supports more effective peace processes. As co-chair of the LC Initiative Fund in 2025, the United Kingdom was proud to champion the efforts to tackle the barriers to women's participation in UN peacekeeping, and we encourage continued progress in this area. Third, peacekeeping operations must be equipped for the realities of today's operating environment. Missions should have access to the technologies, capabilities, and training needed to operate safely and effectively. They must also be equipped to navigate an increasingly complex information environment, including facing the growing challenge posed by misinformation and disinformation in conflict settings. We remain concerned by restrictions imposed by some host states on the use of essential equipment. Such restrictions reduce situational awareness, hinder mandate delivery, and limit missions' ability to respond effectively to evolving threats. We also reiterate that assessed contributions should be paid in full and on time without conditions. Effective peacekeeping depends on predictable and sustainable financing. President, the challenges facing peacekeeping are evolving, but the need for effective peacekeeping has not diminished. The United Kingdom stands ready to work with the Secretary-General, the Secretariat and fellow Member States to ensure that UN peace operations remain adaptable, effective and fit for the challenges ahead.

Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. President. and I'd like to begin by thanking the French presidency for having convened this very timely debate on peace operations and I thank the Secretary General of course for his briefing.

His Excellency Javier Martinez archas um the minister of foreign affairs of Panama to this meeting un peacekeeping missions have been amongst the successful and efficient instruments for maintaining international peace and security. And that they welcomes the publication of the review of all forms of future peace operations, which should serve as a clear catalyst to mobilize our collective efforts in this regard. Operating alongside the United Nations, regional and member states actors, they are one part of a broader complex puzzle. And when considering why no new UN peacekeeping missions have been deployed for more than a decade, We therefore must assess the nature of current conflicts and the role of the United Nations in addressing these conflicts. This role is changing as a result also of multiplication of factors involved in peacemaking, with regional organizations often assuming a leading position. And the ongoing UN reform efforts, together with the selection process for the next Secretary General, offer an opportunity for the United Nations to better identify the comparative advantages and reassert a proactive role for peacekeeping. At the same time, we must ensure that United Nations peacekeeping remains up to date and capable of operating in complex political and security environments. So let me outline three points in this regard. First, mission mandates crafted and approved by the Council play a crucial role in determining mission's success. There have been long-standing calls for clear political objectives, more targeted, realistic, and context-adapted mandates, well-timed and clear exit strategies, and adequate resources. Yet opportunities to pursue these goals have not always been seized. Now, going forward, each mandate renewal should be informed by objective assessments of results and remaining needs, measuring performance against clear benchmarks, not merely activities. And this requires sufficient time and space for proper consultations among council members and a clear picture of available options, and above all, unity of purpose among the members of this council. Furthermore, mission requirements may shift considerably throughout mission's life cycle. Engagement with the host nation is critical to manage expectations and to right-size the missions. Dialogue should also involve host communities who are most affected by mission performance and should have a voice in determining the mission's future. Missions may not require radical adjustments during each renewal cycle, but mandate rollovers should be the exception rather than the norm. The commitment expressed in the review to a more proactive role for the Secretariat during mandate renewals will be essential to reinvigorate this process. Second, Missions must be tailored to exact circumstances they face. Whether their role is limited to a ceasefire monitoring or involves multidimensional presence, mission design should reflect the political and security challenges on the ground rather than follow predetermined blueprints. While we second the aspiration toward lighter and more mobile mission footprints, we also recognize that some key tasks, such as protection of civilians, are often more resource intensive than others. We therefore encourage the study on key military and police capabilities initiated by the review to pursue such an approach. The rigid distinction between peacekeeping missions and special political missions may also merit further reflection, as a coherent peace operations toolbox requires these instruments to be used complementarily in a way that avoids duplication. And no matter what the mission's tasks may be, they should be matched with adequate resources. while ensuring clear accountability for performance and measurable impact. This also requires the readiness to adjust when they no longer meet their mandated objectives or conclude missions in line with credible exit strategies. Third, while the transformation of UN peacekeeping depends first and foremost on political commitments, leveraging technology will be critical to turning this aspiration into reality. We need to ensure that missions become more effective in an operational environment marked by increasing use of AI, cyber tools, drones, and information campaigns by state and non-state actors alike. Technological adaptation is a complex task shaped by relations with host nations, the technical capabilities of troop and police contributing countries, as well as planning and resource management at the UN level. The approach must therefore be comprehensive, covering capabilities, training, and mission-wide integration, while also being agile to keep pace with the rapid technological advancements. And the success in this endeavor will depend on a change in mindset rather than administrative adjustments. President, to conclude, the task of adapting UN peacekeeping is immense. Yet this instrument has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to evolve, and this moment should be no different. Our success will depend on the commitment and engagement of the Security Council members, the Secretariat, troop and police contributing countries, host nations, and international partners. As both a Security Council member and a TCC, Latvia remains committed to playing an active role in these efforts throughout our Council term. Thank you.
I thank Latvia for their statement. I now give the floor to the representative of China.

President, I thank Secretary-General Guterres for the briefing. UN peacekeeping operations came into being for peace and continue to exist for peace. They are effective tools for maintaining international peace and security. At present, with changes unseen in a century accelerating in the world, The situation facing international peace and security being complex and challenging, and all kinds of protracted and fluctuating conflicts, peacekeeping operations are faced with new circumstances, new challenges, and new requirements. Recently, the Secretary-General submitted the report on the review of peace operations, which is of great significance to promoting the transformation, upgrading, better quality, and greater effectiveness and efficiencies of PKOs. I will make four points. First, peacekeeping operations should serve political processes and be kept on the right course. PKOs are ultimately about creating conducive conditions for political settlement and should serve clear-cut political processes. We should fully leverage the roles of preventive diplomacy, good offices, mediation, and political dialogue to bridge political differences, identify the framework of solutions, provide PKOs with a solid political foundation, and avoid ending up with no peace to keep. This is the fundamental guarantee for PKOs to achieve tangible results. At the same time, PKOs should effectively fulfill functions such as protection of civilians and ensuring humanitarian access to minimize the secondary harm caused by conflict. Second, mandates should be optimized and streamlined on the basis of actual needs. When formulating mandates, the Security Council should be grounded in reality and take into full account the nature of the conflict, the environment of the mission, and the needs of the host country to determine the tasks, objectives, and priorities in a solid manner and ensure that the mandates are clear, well-focused, practical, and feasible. We need to further improve the review and assessment mechanism. And in light of the will of the host countries and changes in the situation on the ground, make timely adjustments to the scope and priorities of mandates. We should set clear and feasible transition and exit strategies for PKOs in a timely manner. Yet such strategies should not be held hostage to the policies of any individual country. And no selectivity should be practiced on peacekeeping missions. Third, we should keep improving quality and efficiency and ensure the match between mandates and resources. On one hand, mission should be made more agile, flexible, and efficient. A culture of efficiency should be promoted throughout the entire process. Resource allocation should be continuously optimized. The use of funds should be more cost-effective, and efforts must be made towards greater cost-effectiveness and transparency in the procurement of peacekeeping supplies. The performance assessment system of missions should be improved by valuing the views of the countries concerned and turning the results of the assessments into the basis for improving the ways of operations, enhancing their effectiveness, and reducing expenditures. On the other hand, on the basis of actual needs of mandates, new technology should be leveraged in an active and prudent manner to enhance capabilities such as situational awareness, early warning, and logistical guarantees. And the integration of green, energy-saving, and unmanned intelligent technologies into peacekeeping should be promoted to strengthen the effectiveness of PKOs and the capacity to ensure their own safety and security. The liquidity issue remains a bottleneck constraining PKOs. Member States should provide PKOs with necessary resources. Fourth, we need to strengthen coordination among partners to build synergy for peacekeeping. PKOs are a systematic endeavor. We should further strengthen the communication and cooperation among the Security Council, the Secretariat, the host countries, TCCs, PCCs, and financial contributors to ensure that all parties will coordinate closely, support each other, and work in the same direction, and to improve the links between mandates, implementation of operations, resource guarantee, and strategic assessments. We need to enhance coordination and cooperation with regional organizations such as the African Union, support solving regional problems the regional way through regional strength. support AU and other regional organizations in improving their own peacekeeping capacity, and support the implementation of Security Council Resolution 2719 to fund the AU-led peace support operations. President, China is a firm supporter of and active participant in UN peacekeeping. For more than 30 years, China has sent over 50,000 peacekeepers, participated in 29 UN peacekeeping operations mandated by this Council, established an 8,000-strong peacekeeping standby force, and taken the lead in setting up the world's first standby peacekeeping formed police unit. More than 20 Chinese peacekeepers have made the ultimate sacrifice for peacekeeping operations. We're ready to work with all parties to be guided by the global governance initiative proposed by President Xi Jinping, stay true to the commitment to multilateralism, never forget the mission of maintaining peace, stay grounded in reality, and uphold fundamental principles and break new ground, and make peacekeeping operations more pragmatic, efficient, and sustainable, and make greater contributions to the maintenance of international peace and security. I thank you, President.
I thank the representative of China for this statement. I now give the floor to the representative of the Kingdom of Bahrain.

Thank you, Mr. President. At the outset, I would like to thank the Secretary-General, Mr. Guterres, for his valuable briefing. I welcome the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Panama, Mr. Javier Peters, in this session. Here, I would like to thank all those working in peacekeeping operations. And we convey our condolences and sympathy to those who have lost their lives in the line of duty, as well as my deep gratitude to all Member States contributing troops to peacekeeping operations. In this regard, the Kingdom of Bahrain renews its call to build on Security Council resolution 2823 concerning the protection of peacekeeping personnel from any attacks directed against them. Mr. President, the Kingdom of Bahrain welcomes the issuance of the Secretary-General's report on the review on the future of all forms of United Nations peace operations as one of the outcomes of the Pact for the Future. The Kingdom of Bahrain also expresses its concern at the fact that the world is currently witnessing the highest number of conflicts since 1945, as well as a rise in the number of deaths resulting from armed conflicts over the past five years. These have reached levels exceeding those recorded over the entire 20-year period preceding the year 2021. The Kingdom of Bahrain affirms that peacekeeping operations are of great importance today amid increasingly complex circumstances. They undertake tasks of peacemaking and mediation, the protection of civilians in situations of conflict, securing ceasefire agreements, as well as following up on their implementation. This is in addition to supporting national efforts to restore stability and build and sustain peace in cooperation with relevant regional partners. Mr. President, the Kingdom of Bahrain underscores the importance of providing the resources necessary to enable peacekeeping operations to implement their mandates effectively, while ensuring the optimal use of available resources and enhancing efficiency, accountability, and financial sustainability, in a manner that ensures resources are directed towards the priorities and tasks that achieve tangible impact on the ground. In this connection, the Kingdom of Bahrain has been committed to supporting the effort undertaken by peacekeeping operations for nearly eight decades, a commitment reflected in the Kingdom's payment of its assessed contributions to the approved budgets of peacekeeping missions in full and on time over the past years. Mr. President, the Kingdom of Bahrain calls for strengthening the partnership between the Secretariat host states and enhancing cooperation with regional and sub-regional organizations through the sharing of responsibilities and the exchange of support, expertise and relevant information. In this regard, the Kingdom of Bahrain sees the importance of formulating a political compact as a consensus-based tool among the Security Council, the host State, and the Secretariat, in a manner that contributes to strengthening joint effort towards achieving the desired security and stability. Mr. President, the clarity and flexibility of the objectives and mandates of peacekeeping operations, the transparency of their implementation timelines, the importance of conducting periodic reviews and evaluations of these mandates, their adaptability to emerging challenges, and ensuring the optimal use of available financial and human resources all contribute to achieving the maximum possible impact of these operations on the ground. In this regard, the continuous review of the mandates and objectives of peacekeeping operations and working to develop them during the process of adopting mandate renewal resolutions is of particular importance. Mr. President, the Kingdom of Bahrain welcomes the expanded use of technology in peacekeeping operations, given its contribution to enhancing the capacity of these operations to adapt to various and diverse challenges and threats. The Kingdom of Bahrain calls for continued investment in technology and infrastructure required for peacekeeping operations and in their host states. along with the establishment of innovative partnerships in this regard. In closing, the Kingdom of Bahrain will continue to support all efforts aimed at strengthening joint action in support of peacekeeping operations in a manner that serves security, stability, and peace at both the regional and international levels. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of Bahrain for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Liberia.

Thank you, Mr. President. Liberia joins in thanking the Secretary General for his very thoughtful and insightful briefing. And we welcome the participation of the distinguished Foreign Minister of Panama. Excellencies, Liberia is proof that peacekeeping works. But we are proof of something more precise. Peacekeeping works as a spectrum, not a single instrument. In 1990, ECOMOG intervened to stop our war. In 1993, UNOMIL observed our fragile peace. In 2003, UNMIL kept the peace. By 2018, Liberia carried it alone. Four instruments, one country, one continuum, Because the objective determined the tool, not the other way around. The lesson for us is simple. Peace is not built by one hammer and every crisis is not a nail. That is the first lesson we bring to the four questions this council has posed today. First, on new forms of peacekeeping for modern crisis, the question before us should not be whether the United Nation deploys a mission, but what form of engagement best meets the political and security realities on the ground. Preventive diplomacy, a special political mission, a peacekeeping operation, or a council-authorized regional arrangement. Liberia has lived this full continuum. From ECOMOG to UNAMIL to UNMIL, and ultimately to national ownership, our experience demonstrates that effectiveness lies not in choosing one instrument over another, but in matching the tool to the task. We therefore encourage the Council to recognize this continuum as a matter of doctrine, not ad hoc practice. Peacekeeping should be designed as a bridge out of conflict, strong enough to carry a nation toward stability, but never intended to become its destination. Second, on sharper, better-tailored mandates. Mandates must be clearer. leaner, and more honest about what peacekeeping can deliver and certainly what the situation on the ground requires. When a mandate promises everything, it risks protecting too little, prioritizing too late, and exiting without a plan. Peacekeeping should concentrate on political facilitation, protection of civilians, and security stabilization, while governance and development tasks are carried by the UN country team and national institutions. At each renewal, the Council should ask, what has changed? What is still unfinished? What must now change in the mandate? Liberia proposes mandatory joint transition compacts negotiated at least two years before drawdown with measurable benchmarks, including youth reintegration. Our experience is clear. Peace endured when young people were treated as citizens and partners in recovery, not as risks to be managed. A peace that leaves its youth behind is a peace still waiting to be secured. Third, on genuine dialogue with host countries. Consent cannot be a signature at the start and a formality at the end. Consent must be a conversation, a continuing one, and not a ceremony. We propose a structured political dialogue between the Council, the Secretariat, and host governments at deployment, at every major mandate adjustment, and at transition so that national ownership shapes a mission from its first day, not merely its last. Liberia's own transition succeeded because it was negotiated with us at each stage, not announced to us. Fourth, on technology. The Brahimi Report told this Council a quarter century ago that the Secretariat must tell it what it needs to know, not what it wants to hear. Liberia knows what that discipline requires in practice. Our own response to Ebola succeeded because real-time, community-level data reached decision-makers before the outbreak outran them. We call for extending peace operations technology and readiness framework, secure communications, geospatial analysis, early warning systems, and responsible use of emerging technologies. funded as a line item, not as an afterthought. In modern peacekeeping, information delayed can become protection denied. Technology must serve political judgment, not substitute for it. Mr. President, this organization has just adopted A $5.1 billion peacekeeping budget, 10% lower than last year. Discipline is welcome. But discipline without direction is retreat, not reform. Resolution 2719 remains a framework still waiting on its financing. up to 75% of AU-led operations covered by assessed contributions and 25% still unresolved nearly three years after its adoption. If this Council expects regional partners to shoulder global burdens, it must close that gap and do so now, not at the next crisis. Liberia agrees with the Secretary-General that predictable mandates require predictable financing. Peace cannot be financed by uncertainty. In conclusion, Mr. President, in our use of the tool of peacekeeping, may we never forget that the measure of this Council's success It's not how many missions it authorizes, but how few nations ever need one again. Liberia is the case study. Let us now make it the standard. Let Liberia's story remind us peacekeeping succeeds best when it makes itself ultimately unnecessary. I thank you for your kind attention.
I thank the representative of Liberia for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Colombia.

Thank you very much, Mr. President. We'd like to thank the Secretary-General for the briefing today. And we'd like to welcome the Foreign Affairs Minister of Panama, His Excellency Mr. Javier Martinez-Acha Vazquez, and thank all of the other delegations for being with us today in the room. Mr. President, there is broad agreement on the diagnosis of the situation before us. While recognizing that peacekeeping operations are valuable tools available to the organization in the discharge of its functions, Substantive adjustments are still needed in order to respond to emerging challenges. These are challenges measured in human lives and which, driven by technological developments, are evolving at a pace that outstrips the ability of geopolitical dynamics and institutional practices to respond. The question is whether the Organization overall is taking the measures necessary to adapt its responses to current needs The report prepared on the future of all United Nations peace operations, prepared by the Secretariat, provides a basis for frank reflection on this issue and also for action. Mr. President, Colombia recalls that operations have taken different forms throughout their history, precisely in response to security challenges. Also, in response to geopolitical dynamics and the prevailing paradigms for addressing conflicts, the current context calls for decisive action, a pragmatic, results-oriented multilateralism, entailing profound reforms within the organization and adjustments to the Council's working practices. In this regard, allow me to highlight four calls that are of particular importance to Colombia. Firstly, the design and continuation of operations must respond to concrete needs on the ground and include clearly defined objectives, and it must have verifiable results. Colombia agrees on the need to strengthen the planning and monitoring of mission performance. Likewise, as a country hosting a significant United Nations presence, we recognize the importance of strengthening coordination so that tasks are carried out by the entities best qualified within the system, avoiding silos, inefficiencies and also duplication. Second, Colombia welcomes the recommendations addressed to the Council concerning the process of drafting and renewing mandates. Membership of this organ entails an enormous degree of responsibility, which must itself also be subject to review and accountability. Likewise, my country would expect the Secretariat to play a proactive role by providing realistic information on progress, impact, obstacles and budgetary implications, thereby strengthening its advisory role to the Council. Along the same lines, my country underscores the importance of consultation and coordination with the host state, ensuring that its views and priorities are taken into account throughout the decision-making cycle. Thirdly, the technological modernization of existing and future missions is an urgent imperative. The review of operations must result in missions having the appropriate capabilities to address threats and strengthen the safety and security of mission personnel. At the same time, we must capitalize on the benefits that technologies can offer peacekeeping in terms of cost-effectiveness, situational awareness, risk analysis, and early warning, including those powered by artificial intelligence. Fourth, we need a coherent institutional response to meet these challenges whilst balancing expectations, resources, and mandates. The publication of the report is a first step in a process requiring the commitment of multiple actors, including the Secretariat, the Council and the General Assembly. Colombia reiterates its readiness to contribute to the discussion in the various forums with a view to a more coordinated and effective international action. Lastly, Mr. President, allow me to conclude by recognizing the milestone represented by the adoption of resolution 2823 on accountability for crimes committed against United Nations peacekeeping personnel and pay tribute to the women and men who have given their lives in the service of peace under the flag of the United Nations. Honouring their memory requires us to renew our commitment to the safety and security of deployed personnel, to justice, and to the fight against impunity. Thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Colombia for his statement. I now give the floor to the representative of the United States.

Thank you, President. Thank you, Secretary-General Guterres, for your briefing, and of course a warm welcome to the Foreign Minister of Panama. The United States welcomes this debate and the opportunity to offer our reflections on the review on the future of all forms of United Nations peace operations. The United States is a leader in stopping conflicts and forging peace deals. We believe that decisive diplomacy backed by real leverage is what actually ends wars. The United Nations, by contrast, is mired by bureaucracy and process, including lengthy reviews and statements when addressing conflicts actually requires timely, concrete adaptation. Peacekeeping is no exception. This review, however, does little to address current conflict realities or adapt peacekeeping. Successful peacekeeping demands clear mandates, real accountability, and articulated benchmarks to work towards, not indefinite mandate renewals that substitute for strategy. If I can put this another way, The work we do here in New York must be worthy of the brave women and men working in the field, the civilians they work to protect, and of course, the taxpayers, the hardworking taxpayers who make all of this work possible. So let me be direct. We have lost confidence that peacekeeping, as we currently design and resource it, delivers results proportionate to its cost and footprint. We must rigorously assess missions and hold them accountable for defined outcomes. The United States therefore seeks reform organized around five principles. First, the secretariat and mission leadership must provide unvarnished feedback to this council. The review itself repeats, as our colleague from Liberia pointed out, the review itself repeats the Brahimi report's central assertion The Secretariat must tell the Council what it needs to know, not what it wants to hear. Candor gives Council members the ability to adapt mission priorities as circumstances evolve. This candor includes specific recommendations from the Secretariat so the Council can effectively reconfigure or terminate underperforming missions when needed. For example, recently, the secretariat produced a report that was supposed to detail plans for a missions transition and drawdown. Instead, what we received detailed very little. We asked for tangible plans, not prose about process. Second, the secretariat must develop genuine, integrated mission-level planning. We are pleased to see other countries agree on this. as well as on the importance of establishing a strategic vision and viable end state at a mission's inception. Missions need to have realistic and achievable goals, and as the review recommends, we must be willing to terminate missions that fail to adapt. Third, mandates must stay focused on security functions in service to a political plan, as highlighted in the Secretary General's recommendations in the review. The council must stop adding superfluous language to resolutions that lead to lengthy, unfocused mandates. These efforts veer missions off course by miring them in political niceties instead of focusing them on core efforts. Fourth, the review makes a critical point regarding the need to enhance accountability for performance and conduct. The Council must collectively demand that all stakeholders in peacekeeping uphold high performance standards and address misconduct. This includes the rigorous application of the zero tolerance policy for sexual exploitation and abuse. Deployment eligibility and continued participation in the mission must hinge on these standards. We expect the Secretariat and all contributing countries to match rhetoric with action. Fifth, we demand continued strategic cost efficiencies across UN peacekeeping, especially where cuts do not undermine a mission's ability to implement its mandate. The UN80 Initiative savings that this review cites are a starting point, but not a finish line. Good stewardship of U.S. taxpayer dollars requires greater efficiency and accountability in how the secretariat manages peacekeeping funds. Our support depends on demonstrated results and responsible use of assessed contributions. When missions are stretched thin, that is generally a function of poor prioritization, not insufficient resources. So let there be no ambiguity, peacekeeping has grown too big and too broad. It is trying to do too much. Peacekeeping missions as currently constituted are not unqualified successes. Rather, they are flawed instruments in need of fundamental reform. We call on this Council to match our resolve and restore peacekeeping to its foundational purpose of maintaining international peace and security, and to do so with the urgency that this moment demands. I thank you.
I thank the representative of the United States for their statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Somalia.

Mr. President, I thank France for convening this important and timely debate, and the Secretary-General for his insightful briefing. We welcome the presence of His Excellency Mr. Vasquez, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Panama, in this meeting, and other distinguished representatives joining us today. Allow me to begin by paying tribute to the women and men serving under the United Nations flag, often in extremely difficult conditions. We honor those who have made the ultimate sacrifice. As Somalia approaches the end of its tenure on this Council, one lesson is clear: peacekeeping succeeds or fails long before a peacekeeper enters the field. It begins with our political decisions, the clarity of our mandates, the unity of this Council, and our willingness to match expectations with adequate resources. The Secretary-General's review on the future of United Nations peace operations offers a sobering assessment. Conflicts are multiplying, increasingly internationalized, protracted, and technologically advanced, while geopolitical divisions continue to constrain collective action. No new United Nations peacekeeping operations has been established since 2014. Peace operations remain relevant, but we must ask, whether we are creating the political conditions necessary for their success. For Somalia, we have seen what international solidarity can achieve when grounded in national ownership and guided by clear political objectives. We also know the human cost when mandates, resources, and political realities fall out of alignment. Against this backdrop, allow me to make five points. First, politics and prevention must come first. Peace operations cannot manufacture political will or substitute for a genuine commitment to dialogue. We must make fuller use of Chapter VI tools systematically, offering good offices, fact-finding, and Article 34 engagement. As highlighted in the review, small regional offices and envoys provide cost-effective preventative diplomacy. Prevention's true value is measured in conflicts avoided, families not displaced, and children spared from becoming refugees. Second, partnership with host states must be strengthened. Operations are most effective when built on trust, sustained consultation, and respect for national sovereignty. Host states must play a central role across missions design, mandate reviews, and transitions. Establishing compacts on mutual commitments can clarify operational parameters as well as capabilities. Ultimately, partnerships should reinforce national institutions to enable host countries to assume full responsibility for sustaining peace. Third, mandates must be realistic, prioritized, and adaptable. The Security Council must use mandate renewals to assess progress, incorporate new priorities, or discontinue unachievable tasks. Transition planning and exit strategies must be embedded from the mission's inception. accompanied by an early division of labor with the United Nations country team to consolidate peacebuilding gains. Such clear frameworks ensure missions leave behind stronger and enduring national capacities. Fourth, efficiency and adequate resourcing must go hand in hand. Peacekeepers facing drones, improvised explosive devices, cyber threats, and disinformation require enhanced mobility, situational awareness, and appropriate technology. Efficiency must not become another word for under-resourcing. We cannot authorize ambitious mandates and then de-prioritize missions mandate in achieving the means and ways to implement them. Therefore, Member States must pay assessed contribution in full and on time. Streamlining administrative structures under UN Aid Initiative must never translate into under-resourcing, nor can financial liquidity crisis compromise peacekeeper safety or operational delivery. Attacks against United Nations personnel must also be investigated and prosecuted consistent with Resolution 2823. Fifth, and my last point, cooperation with regional and sub-regional organizations must be deepened. For Somalia and Africa, the partnership between United Nations and the African Union remains vital. Regional arrangements bring essential proximity, legitimacy, and operational capability. Resolution 2719 provides an indispensable framework for predictable, adequate, and sustainable financing for African-led peace support operations. The Council should proactively operationalize this landmark framework on a case-by-case basis. To conclude, Mr. President, when a mission completes its mandate and lowers the United Nations flag, its legacy should be assessed not by the duration of its presence, but by whether the host nation is more resilient and equipped to sustain peace and development. Somalia reaffirms its commitment to working constructively with the United Nations, the African Union, TCCs, and all partners to advance peace operations that are effective, nationally owned, and capable of delivering sustainable peace.
I thank the representative of Somalia for his statement, and I give the floor to the representative of Greece.

At the outset, I would like to thank the Secretary-General for his valuable briefing, and I welcome the participation of the Foreign Minister of Panama to this meeting. UN peace operations remain one of the most visible and effective tools to maintain international peace and security. We want to pay tribute to the courage and dedication of the Blue Helmets, the men and women who serve under the UN flag, often in extremely difficult conditions, far from home. We honour the memory of those who have paid the ultimate price in the line of duty. Attacks against peacekeepers are unacceptable and constitute serious violations of Security Council resolutions and international law. And in this regard, we welcome the unanimous adoption of Resolution 2823. Mr. President, in today's increasingly complex environment, peace operations need to adapt. We should be open to different approaches when circumstances require them. The recently deployed Gang Suppression Force in Haiti is one example of a new hybrid model. Such arrangements may not work everywhere, but they broaden the options available to us. At the same time, the Council must retain its central role in mandating and overseeing peace operations. I wish to highlight four points in this regard. First. The review gives us a useful roadmap for adapting peace operations to today's realities. We need mandates that are clear and achievable, rather than mandates that try to address everything. But adaptation should not come at the expense of the core tasks of peacekeeping, including monitoring ceasefires and protecting civilians. Missions also need clear political objectives and from the outset a realistic sense of how they will eventually transition or draw down. Second, technology can help. Artificial intelligence in particular can improve situational awareness, make operations more effective, and help keep our personnel safe. UAVs are one example, but we should also be clear about the risks. The same technologies can be used to spread disinformation, manipulate information, and target or discredit peacekeepers. Their use must therefore remain consistent with international law, human rights, and accountability. Third, the Security Council must play its part. We should translate the relevant recommendations of the review into our own practice. This means, among other things, listening more closely to host states, both when missions are established and when their mandates are reviewed. Above all, peace operations must remain politically driven. They cannot substitute for a viable political process. Fourth. Peacekeeping cannot succeed without strong partnerships. We need close cooperation among the UN, host countries, local communities, troop and police contributing countries, and regional organizations, including the African Union. The next peacekeeping ministerial, to be hosted by Indonesia and the Netherlands in Jakarta, will be an important opportunity to strengthen these partnerships. In conclusion, Mr. President, The future of UN peace operations will depend not only on the tools we develop, but on whether we have the political will to use them. We need peace operations that can adapt, that enjoy political support, that have the resources to do their job, and that remain firmly grounded in the UN Charter and international law. Greece will continue to work with the Secretary-General, the Secretariat, and with all Council members to strengthen UN peace operations and take forward the recommendations of this review. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Greece for their statement and I'll give the floor to the representative of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Mr. President, the Democratic Republic of the Congo thanks the French Presidency for organizing this debate on the issue that directly affects the credibility and capacity for action of our organization. We also thank the Secretary-General of the United Nations for his presentation and recommendations, and we welcome the presence of Mr. Javier Martinez Acha Vazquez, His Excellency, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Panama. The Democratic Republic of the Congo, which hosts on its territory one of the oldest and largest peacekeeping operations, is following with particular attention the reflections on their future. And we do so not as observers, but on the basis of more than two decades of experience with its achievements, difficulties, sometimes disappointments, but also with the conviction that peacekeeping remains one of the most valuable instruments at the UN. And this experience invites us to beware of overly simple answers. Indeed, in the face of protracted conflicts, changing security environments and scarce resources, the Streamlining can be great to measure the effectiveness of an operation by solely reducing its footprint, its personnel, or its costs. For my delegation, however, streamlining does not mean giving up. A less endowed mission is not necessarily a more effective one. It can simply become a mission less capable of discharging the mandate from this Council. The observation that there is sometimes no real peace to maintain cannot in itself exhaust our reflection on the relevance of the UN presence. Rather, it should lead us to question the nature of this presence, the instruments it mobilizes, and its ability to evolve with the conflict it is called upon to accompany. and the establishment of lasting peace. The experience of our country has taught us a great deal, in particular that the trajectory of peace operation is never linear, that the circumstances can lead a host state to consider a gradual reduction in an international presence, can change abruptly when threats we thought contained reemerge or a new security situation emerges. And that is why We plead for the transitions to be responsible, concerted, and above all, reversible when the realities on the ground require it to be so. It seems to us, therefore, that the real question is no longer just how to maintain peace, but how to enable the United Nations operation to more effectively cover the entire path to peace. When peace exists, it must be possible to preserve it. When it remains fragile, it must be consolidated. And when it moves away, we must have the political and diplomatic instruments to recreate the conditions for it. It is guided by this that my delegation sees particular potential in much closer articulation between peacekeeping, peacebuilding, prevention, and mediation. The clarity of mandate should not be an impediment to the assessment of the situation. It needs to guide its progress and guide the reassessment of its potential instruments. Generally speaking, peacekeeping should be basing itself also on the political tools of this organization, support the mediation process, help with the ceasefire, and create the political space necessary for the settlement of conflict.
