Our experience confirmed us in this. MONUSCO participation in the joint verification mechanism and others shows how existing mechanisms can use their mechanisms for a broader security architecture. It's not just keeping the acquired peace, but making sure that a lasting peace can be maintained. Mr. President, this adaptation of peace operations cannot be thought without the host state for the mission. For the DRC, this is a fundamental principle. The consent of the host state cannot be viewed as a formality at the time of deployment and then eventually relegated to the background. It has to fuel the entire mission, the definition of its priorities, the development of the mandate, deployment, reconfiguration, and the conditions for its transition. Peace operations are only cannot be successful when there is a gap between the environment and the state's needs. The partnership with the host state has to be permanent, substantive, and based on shared responsibility. The future of peace operations must be worked out together with the host states. This also means that the mandates have to be provided with the means that they need, and the liquidity crisis is not an abstract accounting difficulty. It is expressed on the ground through lesser presence in some areas, different reaction times, and definite consequences for civilian population, which means that other missions need to have the means to implement their mandate. We therefore need to be a predictable funding mechanisms. and also when they're conducted by regional organizations. And we think that resolution 2719 need to be given its full expression. Lastly, rethinking peace operations also means that we need to protect those who are serving on the UN banner. Attacks against the blue helmets and the civilians of the United Nations, restrictions on their freedom of movement and arbitrary detention are all diminishing our capacity to act. The Government of the DRC, therefore, is constantly recalling that the freedom of movement of MONUSCO, its access to various areas, such as the M23 areas, remain essential for the fulfilment of its mandate. Mr. President, in conclusion, The Democratic Republic of the Congo believes that the future of peacekeeping should not be reduced to a choice between maintaining the architectures of yesterday and reducing the presence of the United Nations of tomorrow. It must be one of transformation, a transformation that allows our operations to move from peacekeeping to peacebuilding when the circumstances require, from protection to support to mediation, from the observance of a ceasefire to support for the mechanisms that make it possible to preserve it. A transformation that makes regional organizations true partners. And above all, a transformation that keeps the host state at the heart of any decision affecting the evolution of an international presence on its territory. Because conflicts evolve, and therefore the path that leads to peace change with them. Our operation must be able to evolve with our commitment to peace remaining. I thank you.
I thank the representative of the Democratic Republic of the Congo for their statement. I now give the floor to the representative of the Russian Federation.

Mr. President, we thank the French presidency for organizing the traditional Security Council's debate on UN nations -- United Nations peacekeeping operations. We listened very carefully to the Secretary General's assessment of the state of affairs in this area. Today, when the line surrounding war and peace is becoming increasingly blurred and long-term conflict resolution is often being replaced by palliative measures, when armed groups have gained access to technologies that we previously thought were the privileges of individual states, At this time, adaptation of the UN to contemporary reality is particularly relevant. And we see a worthwhile attempt to launch a process of rethinking approaches to UN peacekeeping in the recently issued review of the future of all UN peace operations, which we already had an opportunity to discuss in August during the Danish presidency of the Council. Peacekeeping now is going through difficult times. the number of missions and the number of blue helmets is decreasing. And the reasons for that are varied. The liquidity crisis directly linked to the failure of certain member states to meet their budgetary obligations, declining confidence on the part of host countries, and in some cases, changing geopolitical realities. The fact that since 2014, not a single new peacekeeping mission has been deployed is not evidence of problems with the effectiveness of the UN in this area, but rather the result of a whole range of factors and not always directly related to UN activities. We think it's wise to focus the discussion on what can realistically be changed in the work of peacekeeping missions in order to bring them into line with present-day realities. First and foremost, we should finally, definitely move away from the paradigm that has proved ineffective, the paradigm in which peacekeeping missions are viewed as a tool used to transform a host state in accordance with certain international standards. The purpose of PKOs, as rightly noted in the review of the future of all UN peace operations, is to support the peace process or to create conditions for a political settlement. Any assistance in state building should be provided only at the request of the host state with a strict respect for state sovereignty. And this brings us to one of the key recommendations of the review regarding the fundamental importance for the effective functioning of the missions of consent and cooperation with the host state, which bears primary responsibility for the security of its population. And this also means the need to be receptive to justified criticism from national authorities and local populations, which should be taken as guidance for action, rather. It is important to understand that disinformation, the need to combat which is often discussed within these walls, is only powerful when it is at least partially based on truth. We would also like to note the long overdue need for serious work on focusing peacekeeping mission mandates on priority tasks directly related to security and politics. In the context of the ongoing liquidity crisis, when thousands of peacekeepers are returning home solely for financial reasons, such functions as human rights monitoring, promotion of women in local government bodies, or monitoring climate change are becoming an unaffordable luxury. We are confident that specialized UN entities can handle these tasks perfectly well if requested by the host state to do so. Russia, as a responsible permanent member of the Security Council, will continue in practice to advocate for clear and realistic mandates aimed at advancing political settlement and achieving national reconciliation through the unique advantages of the Blue Helmets, which are unavailable to any other forms of UN presence. And above all, This concerns the doctrine characteristics of UN peacekeeping, which are based on the UN Charter and the three fundamental principles, namely consent of the parties, impartiality, and the use of force exclusively in self-defense and defense of the mandate. Only this enables the Blue Helmets to play their unique role in creating the conditions necessary for the sustainable resolution of crises. Mr. President, We have consistently been proceeding from the understanding that the optimal forum for discussing major trends in peacekeeping has been and remains the Special Committee on Peacekeeping Operations of the General Assembly, whose strength lies in the principle of consensus. The final word on reforms in this area should remain with States. Attempts to substitute decisions of Member States with some kind of creative initiatives, including those of the UN Secretariat, such as its Action for Peacekeeping initiative and its subsequent iterations, they are unacceptable. Mr. President, in conclusion, We would like to reaffirm our commitment to active participation in UN peacekeeping activities. 54 Russian nationals are serving in the organization's missions in Africa and the Middle East, in Latin America, and in Cyprus. Russia is among the top 10 contributors to peacekeeping operation budgets. And on a continuous basis, we train both Russian and foreign multidisciplinary specialists, including women, and personnel from defense and law enforcement agencies at the centers of -- centers certified by the UN Secretariat. And these are centers of the Ministry of Defense and the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Russian Federation. I thank you for your attention.

I thank the representative of the Russian Federation for his statement. And I will now make my statement as a representative of France. I would like to begin by thanking the Secretary-General for the study on peace operations, as well as for his briefing today. And France would like to express our thanks to all personnel serving in peace operations, as well as thank the troop and police contributing countries for their essential role. And I'd like to pay tribute to the memory of those who have paid the ultimate sacrifice in the service of peace and the United Nations. We are currently living through a paradoxical time. Despite the resurgence of conflicts around the world and the continued political support enjoyed by peacekeeping, it is losing momentum as a peacekeeping operation. There can be no doubt, however, that guaranteeing international peace is the main raison d'etre of the United Nations, and that peace operations, in all of their diversity, are the most effective instrument that this Council has to act. France fully endorses one of the principal findings of the study of the Secretary-General: Namely, peace operations are, first and foremost, political instruments. Their successes and failures are determined primarily by the political processes they are mandated to support. It is also essential to mobilize the resources necessary for the implementation of mandates, which notably requires all Member States to pay their contributions in full and on time. This is the obligation that they have, according to their commitments. France welcomes the contribution made by this study to the reform of peacekeeping, and we thank the Department of Peace Operations and the Department of Political Affairs, as well as the Secretariat overall, for their work. We would like the Council to work more specifically in the future around three basic areas. First, greater agility, modernization, and diversification. Firstly, agility. On the basis of agile analysis by the Secretariat of the situations on the ground and appropriate planning, the Council must be able to review mandates whenever circumstances so require. This means developing our capacity to restructure missions and to move swiftly from one peace operation model to another in order to better respond to the complexity of the threats and situations. This is the rationale behind the concept of a spectrum of peace operations within which peacekeeping operations retain their full relevance. Second, better access to technology. In order to strengthen the operational effectiveness of missions, This requires human, logistical, and financial resources better adapted to the pace and increasingly challenging nature of operational environments. The review proposed in the study of the key capabilities required by operations must be a priority. Thirdly, diversification. Diversification of operational approaches. This requires the strengthening of a culture of partnerships and promoting interoperability. The operation in Haiti is a good illustration of this. And with regard to operations linked to regional organizations, the African Union is a major partner, and the implementation of Resolution 2719 remains a priority whenever circumstances are conducive to it. Colleagues, France also attaches particular importance to security of blue helmets and we firmly condemn any attacks on them and we welcome the unanimous adoption of Resolution 2723 at the initiative of Denmark and Pakistan this year, strengthening our... means to combat attacks on peacekeepers. I will conclude by recalling the many comparative advantages enjoyed by the UN in the field of peacekeeping: the ability to mobilize capacities and resources rapidly; the political legitimacy of the Security Council and its impartiality; the commitment and experience of troop and police contributing countries; comparatively lower costs and recognized technical and normative expertise. These advantages remain. France recently co-chaired, together with Morocco, the second ministerial conference on peacekeeping in French-speaking environments that was held in Rabat on the 20th of May. We will continue to work with all states involved in peace operations to adapt them to contemporary challenges and to make them a renewed instrument. in the service of international peace and security. I resume my functions as President of the Council, and I now give the floor to the representative of Indonesia.

Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, let me begin by thanking France for convening this important debate. I also thank the Secretary-General for his insightful briefing. Excellencies, peacekeeping operations have long stood as a symbol of multilateralism at its best. embodying the credibility and legitimacy of these organizations. In 1957, Indonesia deployed its first peacekeepers to preserve international peace and security. Since then, over 60,000 Indonesian finest sons and daughters have served across peacekeeping operations worldwide. While the global security environment has transformed, Indonesia's pride in peacekeeping remains steadfast. Peacekeeping operations must evolve to become more agile, adaptive, cost-efficient and fit for the future. Above all, our strategy must be anchored in the fundamental conviction that peacekeeping must support political solutions. I wish to highlight three priorities. First, ensuring an inclusive, Member State-driven, for implementing the Secretary-General's review on the future for all forms of UN peace operations. We welcome the Secretary-General's report on the review on the future of all forms of UN peace operations, which precisely underlines that peace operations can only succeed with the political support from the Council through clear, achievable mandates. To translate this landmark review into meaningful operational impact, implementation must be guided by a spirit of shared and inclusive stewardship. The Special Committee on Peacekeeping Operations, C-34, stands as the intergovernmental forum where the voices of troop contributing countries, host states and the broader membership converge. By aligning the work of the C34, the Council and the Secretariat, we ensure that reforms carry genuine ownerships and remain deeply rooted in operational realities on the ground. Second, strengthening deterrence and technology to protect those who protect the peace. Attacks against peacekeepers are unacceptable. For Indonesia, the safety and security of peacekeepers is not an abstract concept. It is a painful reality felt deeply when our own brave personnel made the ultimate sacrifice under the UN flag. We welcome the unanimous adoption of Resolution 2823, which reinforced accountability for crimes committed against UN personnel, establishing credible deterrence against future attacks. Deterrence must also be reinforced by operational capabilities. harnessing digital tools, real-time situation awareness, early warning systems, counter threat technology, and specialized capability to protect personnel on the front lines. To this end, the push for cost efficiency on the context of reform must never justify any arbitrary cost-cutting that compromises adequate resources or personal safety. Third, Indonesia is proud to hosting the upcoming UN Peacekeeping Ministerial toward the end of 2027 in Jakarta, together with the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Indonesia's vision alliance with the Netherlands' longstanding advocacy for more effective UN peacekeeping, including through the A4P, A4P+, and A4P Impact. Indonesia has focused on strengthening community engagement and the safety and security of peacekeepers. while the Netherlands has advanced this agenda by championing protections of civilians and mission performance. We look forward to the support and close cooperation with all Member States to ensure the success of the Ministerial, including its preparatory conferences. Looking ahead, UN peacekeeping must remain an indispensable tool for international peace and security. We stand ready to work with all Member States to ensure that peacekeeping remains effective credible and firmly anchored in the principle of the United Nations. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of Indonesia for his statement, and I give the floor to the representative of Lebanon.

Thank you, Mr. President. Allow me to thank the French presidency for convening this debate. I'd also like to thank the Secretary-General for his briefing and his report, which is coming at a key time for the future of peace operations. We, for our part, are convinced that a reconfiguration of peace operations involves a multilateral approach that is anchored in international law, particularly in the United Nations Charter. I wish to pay tribute to all of those who have served under the blue flag and to those who have given their lives, particularly in the service of UNIFIL. Lebanon will not forget this sacrifice, and there can be no impunity for crimes committed against soldiers of UNIFIL. Since Since 1978, the United Nations force in Lebanon has been part of our daily life. Let us remind ourselves of what UNIFIL is and what it has never claimed to be. Its purpose is not to prevent conflict, nor can it on its own guarantee the absence of violence. Its role is to contain escalation as far as possible. Without it, the situation would have been far more serious. What it has helped achieve is the avoidance of collapse rather than the attainment of peace. It has helped to preserve space for de-escalation through its presence on the ground, through the tripartite mechanism that it facilitates, through its support for humanitarian access, and through its contribution to the protection of civilians. It supports efforts towards a political settlement, and that is the very spirit and the letter of Resolution 1701 of the Security Council. whose full implementation must remain our common objective. A peace operation derives its value only from the political process it serves, never from acting as a substitute for that process, and a lot of speakers that took the floor before me have recalled this today. Mr. President, we have to see that the situation has deteriorated since the adoption of resolution 2790, and particularly since the 2nd of March. We have witnessed the continuation of deadly Israeli attacks, as well as the continued occupation of the south of the country. This is not the time to weaken the instrument tasked with observing, reporting, and supporting efforts on the ground. That is why This transition, when it takes place, must be organized and planned without creating a security vacuum. On the contrary, it must strengthen the presence of the Lebanese state and its institutions, foremost among them the Lebanese Armed Forces. It's for this reason that the government of Lebanon supports the maintenance of a temporary international presence until our Lebanese army is able to fully deploy throughout the territory. In that context, maintaining a United Nations presence remains the preferred option, both operationally and logistically, as well as in terms of cost-effectiveness. We would, of course, wish to see that option embodied in a resolution of this Council. This is also a very concrete expression on the ground of the need for agile mandates and viable transitions, highlighted in the Secretary-General's report. It should also be emphasized that this presence would complement the current discussion process sponsored by the United States. A neutral and credible presence remains in the interest of all parties without exception. We need an impartial mechanism capable of ensuring, over the long term, the monitoring, verification, and reporting of violations of the cessation of hostilities. Finally, we welcome the support provided by all states to our armed forces, and I'm thinking in particular of the ongoing commitment of France, and I think in particular of the meeting held yesterday, the 17th of September, in Paris, in preparation for the international conference in support of the Lebanese armed forces. The Lebanese government intends to shoulder its responsibilities. What it asks of its partners is support. a road map, a clear timetable and a verifiable mechanism for following priorities and measuring their impact over time. Everything we have said is directed towards a single goal: the full sovereignty of the Lebanese State over its entire territory, sovereignty whose benefits extend beyond our borders and could potentially reach the entire region. France itself, speaking from this very chamber in 2017 through your representative, recalled the following: "UNIFIL is a regional public good." That is true. At the same time, we look forward to the day when it will no longer be necessary, the day when that Lebanese sovereignty is fully exercised. That day, more than any other, will mark the success of this mission, a mission, in Lebanon as elsewhere, on which depend lives protected, lines held, and the prospects for peaceful settlements preserved. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Lebanon for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Portugal.

Thank you, Mr. President.

I would like to thank the French presidency for convening this debate on a very important issue, central for the United Nations.

I also welcome the presence of the Foreign Minister of Panama at this meeting.

The detailed briefing and for the comprehensive report. We strongly welcome this comprehensive review that deserves broad support from our side. Our central message is clear and here we break it down into six points. First, primacy of politics must come first. Peace operations need more focus and adaptable mandates as well as greater agility. But flexibility must not become disengagement. When crisis erupts, we should act earlier and adapt faster. Second, mandate renewal should be genuine strategic reviews with clear political objectives, realistic resources and transitions planned from the outset. Third, we need prevention, mediation, good offices and fact-finding missions, including through Article 34. These instruments should be used before crises are then. Fourth, we should also use the full spectrum of peace operations more strategically. Traditional peacekeeping will not always be the right instrument. Special political missions, regional offices, peacekeeping and peacebuilding should be combined or sequenced according to the political objective. Fifth, more adequate division of labor through stronger partnerships, both within UN system, including different agencies, and with regional organizations. Portugal strongly supports deeper UN-African Union cooperation and the effective implementation of Resolution 2719. But partnerships must remain anchored in a coherent political strategy and clear Council responsibility. Sixth and last, we must also ensure the safety and protection of peacekeepers and humanitarian personnel, including through full respect for international humanitarian law. In sum, peace operations must become more political, more strategic, more adaptable and better equipped for increasingly complex and challenging environments. Mr. President, as the Secretary General recently reminded us, no peace operation supported by the United Nations can succeed without solid and cohesive support from member states. Portugal has contributed over 20,000 personnel to UN peacekeeping missions over the last 65 years. As both an incoming member of this Council and a long-standing contributor to the UN peace operations, Portugal will continue to play its part. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Portugal for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Austria.

Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Jerome.

We thank Secretary-General Antonio Guterres for his briefing and welcome his review on the future of all peace operations as an important contribution to making peace operations fit for purpose. I also want to appreciate and acknowledge the presence of Under-Secretary Jean-Pierre Lacroix. As a long-standing troop-contributing country and supporter of UN peacekeeping, Austria considers the future and the credibility of UN peace operations a core priority. We need to remain open to new forms of peace operations, mandated by the Security Council. Austria advocates stronger partnerships with regional organizations, including the African Union and the European Union. We see resolution 2719 as an important step towards predictable, sustainable and flexible financing for AU-led peace support operations and are keen to see it implemented. Second, peace operations must be equipped for the future. New technologies are not only changing the security environment, but also the modalities of peace operations. We must ensure that missions can keep pace and have access to the capabilities they need to protect peacekeepers. At the same time, the Council and the Secretariat should consider more closely how new technologies can be applied to ensure more effective mandate implementation. Third, mandates must remain responsive to realities on the ground. We need a clear, shared vision of what a mission is meant to achieve, along with sustained support from the Security Council, of course. And responsive mandates also require better dialogue with local communities and civil society, with particular attention to the voices of women and youth. Fourth, we need Stronger integrated mission planning. Translating Security Council guidance into effective action requires civilian, police and military components to work towards a shared strategic vision. Integrated planning can strengthen strategic alignment, resource allocation and accountability. Austria has been working with Denmark and with the support of many others, including here on the Council, to advance this issue within existing structures and resources. Finally, implementation of the review should be focused and realistic. Looking ahead, further than planning well, it would make a great difference if we could move forward towards a more integrated review mechanism for peacekeeping missions and special political missions alike. As we prepare to assume our responsibilities on the Council in 2027, Austria will remain a steadfast, constructive and engaged partner in these efforts. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Austria for this statement. I now give the floor to the representative of the African Union.

Mr. President, esteemed members of the Council, the African Union thanks France for convening this debate and the Secretary-General for his briefing and report on the review on the future of all forms of United Nations peace operations. Most United Nations peacekeepers serve in Africa, and most of the operations under review are on the African continent. On behalf of His Excellency Ambassador Mohammed Idris, Permanent Observer of the African Union to the United Nations, I will make the following five quick points. First, three weeks ago in Luanda, Angola, the Assembly of the African Union, in its 21st extraordinary session on conflict prevention, adopted a decision urging this Council to implement Resolution 2719. That is the voice of our continent's highest organ, and it converges with the Secretary-General's report. which frames the resolution as a renewed interpretation of Chapter 8 of the Charter and recommends that this Council act proactively on a case-by-case basis in authorizing support to African Union-led peace support operations. Whilst this resolution notes that AU-led peace support operations and their mandates must be matched with the required support by the UN, It goes beyond enabling predictable and adequate financing and offers greater opportunities for continuous enhancement of AU-UN strategic partnership and cooperation. The task now is implementation. Second, where UN support arrangements are in place for mandated operations that are in transition, the report warns against the abrupt or premature withdrawal of such support. to avoid the risks of reversing hard-won gains. Orderly and predictable successor arrangements must be the alternative. Third, the Luanda Assembly took note of the African Standby Force Strategic Review adopted by the 17th meeting of the African Union Specialised Technical Committee on Defence, Safety and Security. and directed a review of AU peace support operations and development of a peace support operations strategy for presentation to the next AU ordinary summit. In this regard, both the AU and the UN are renewing our instruments in the same season. Alignment between the two reviews and the effective implementation of the recommendations should therefore be the shared ambition. Fourth, Troop and police contributing countries, most of them African, must have a stronger voice in mandate design. Peacekeepers should also be respected by host states, equipped with the technology the report rightly demands, and be fully protected to enable effective mandate implementation. Within this context, the African Union welcomes Resolution 2823 and its full implementation. France has placed youth, peace and security at the heart of their presidency for this month. This resonates with Africa's status as the world's youngest continent. Within this context, the report's first priority is peacemaking, and peacemaking succeeds where young people help to author and commit to sustaining peace. The African Union works to that end through the continental framework on youth, peace and security, its 10-year implementation plan, and the African Youth Ambassadors for Peace Initiative. This review's implementation should therefore carry youth participation into mandates and transitions, alongside the full implementation of the Women, Peace, and Security agenda. Finally, adopting peace operations to current dynamics requires, in the Secretary-General's own words, a more representative Security Council beginning with redress of the historical injustice against Africa. The African Union will include these positions in next month's joint consultations between our two councils and stands ready to work with every member of this council accordingly. Within the same context, the African Union encourages council members to reflect the recommendations addressed to this council in today's debate in your third year review of resolution 2719 by December this year. This offers this Council a golden opportunity to embrace the progress achieved in implementing the resolution's roadmap and align these efforts with the implementation of the recommendations of the UN PSO review with the AU peace support operation strategy directed by the Luanda summit towards further enhancing AU-UN partnership and cooperation to further enhance the conduct of peace operations in Africa and beyond. I thank you.
I thank the representative of the African Union for their statement. I now give the floor to the representative of India.

Thank you, Mr. President, for convening this open debate and for France's stewardship of the Council this month. I also thank the Secretary-General for his remarks. I welcome the presence of the Foreign Minister of Panama. I also acknowledge the presence of USG, Jean-Pierre Lacroix. At the outset, I pay homage to the brave peacekeepers we have lost this year, a reminder of the price our troops pay for the maintenance of international peace and security. India has a long history in UN peacekeeping, deploying nearly 300,000 troops across more than 50 missions, the largest troop contributor to date. 184 Indian peacekeepers have made the supreme sacrifice as blue helmets. Our approach is shaped not by rhetoric, but by their sweat and blood. And in that spirit, we offer these observations. First, we note the Secretary-General's review on the future of peace operations and its call for a reset grounded in peacemaking and political solutions. Peacekeeping remains irreplaceable for its restraint, impartiality, consent and force used only in self-defense of the mandate. Which is why blue helmets are received as protectors, not intervening powers. Second, peace operations succeed when accompanied by a clear political process, with which this Council must stay engaged. Third, mandates must be matched to resources at authorization, so peacekeepers are not asked to do more with less. Fourth, Troop and police contributing countries should have a structured voice in shaping mandates through consultation before they are adopted or reviewed. Fifth, peacekeeper safety is paramount. Personnel face asymmetric, technologically enabled threats, and those who attack them must be held accountable, as reflected in India's leadership on Resolution 2589. Sixth, rationalization is very essential. Aligning host state priorities with mission mandates is needed to ensure that missions do not become long-term auxiliary political instruments. Missions sustained on political life support without operational rationale drain resources that are needed elsewhere and undermine the credibility of peacekeeping as a whole. Seventh. Technology and renewable energy can improve efficiency in achieving mandate goals, and their infusion into peacekeeping must be expedited. Lastly, India has deployed women peacekeepers since 1960 and regards them as central to mandate delivery, reflected in our first all-women formed police unit and three consecutive UN Military Gender Advocate of the Year awards. Mr. President. Because we regard peacekeeping as irreplaceable to this Council's core purpose, India has made it a priority for our Security Council candidacy for 2028-29. We reaffirm our commitment to a peacekeeping architecture better resourced, protected, and representative of the world it serves. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of India for his statement, and I'll give the floor to the representative of Japan.

Thank you, Mr. President. convening this important debate and providing us with the opportunity to participate. First of all, allow me to pay tribute to the peacekeepers who have made the ultimate sacrifice and to extend Japan's condolences to their families and countries. I also thank the Secretary-General, Guterres, for his briefing and welcome his report on the future of all forms of UN peace operations. Peacekeeping operations remain one of the most effective tools available to the UN to promote international peace and security. In responding to the report, let me highlight three points. First, The personnel on the ground play the most critical role in implementing mandates decided by the Security Council. Their safety and capability are paramount. We call on the Council to give due weight to the discussions among troop and police contributing countries, as well as financial contributing countries, in order to ensure that the individual mandates are realistic, focused and effective. The Special Committee on Peacekeeping Operations, or C-34, may serve as the most representative platform for such a discussion. Japan will continue to support UN peacekeeping as one of its major financial contributors and through the efforts to enhance mission effectiveness, including capability-building initiatives in partnership with TCCs and PCCs. Second, Japan believes that peacekeeping can best perform when it is aligned with host states' long-term political objectives. In this regard, a comprehensive approach to peace remains indispensable. It should be grounded in the HDP nexus and built on close and constructive relations between the UN actors, including development and humanitarian agencies, and host states, inclusive of the whole of society. This is in line with the report's call for stronger partnerships with host states and whole of UN response to sustaining peace. Third, in line with the report's call for peace operations to move towards nimbler, more adaptable models, Japan requests the Secretariat in its ongoing review of mission structures and command and control arrangements will also explore closer integration among the civilian, military, and support components of mission headquarters, rather than establishing new coordination bodies. Mr. President, Japan reiterates its continued commitment to the collective effort to shape future UN peace operations, including through the Action for Peacekeeping Initiative and its subsequent implementation frameworks, in solidarity with the Council, TCCs and PCCs, financial contributors, the Secretariat and missions in the field. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Japan for his statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Germany.

Thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you, Mr. President.

To address the Council today and for this very timely meeting. would like to firstly express our appreciation for the many women and men serving in peacekeeping operations around the world, often under very dangerous circumstances. Thank you also to the Secretary-General for his briefing and for the report, the review on the future of all forms of United Nations peace operations. We are proud to have provided input to the review and to have hosted last year's peacekeeping ministerial. where over 140 member states expressed overwhelming political support for peacekeeping. Mr. President, the gap between the potential of peacekeeping as an instrument for conflict resolution in the spirit of true global burden sharing on the one hand, and the practice of peacekeeping operations on the other hand is significant and deserves our attention. So as we start into the discussion of the future of peacekeeping and the follow-up to the SGE report, the leading question is to our mind, How can we design, mandate, and equip missions to make them more effective and assure the necessary political support? And I would like to make two points today, one on substance and one on process and follow-up. On substance, missions require mandates that allow them to succeed on the ground. And we have a collective responsibility to design mandates in a way that allows a mission to achieve tangible and sustainable results first and foremost for the affected population of the host state. That does not mean, to our mind, finding the smallest common denominator or compromising for the sake of agreeing on a mandate. Very concretely, we would suggest that we think more about the following aspect of mandates. For example, using a sequenced approach. starting with a modest, narrowly defined mandate and then widen it as conditions on the ground allow. It could mean utilizing a broader spectrum of mission setups and configuration as described in the independent study on the future of peacekeeping which was prepared for the Berlin Ministerial. We could look at limited presence that would be more appropriate or in other cases we could look at setting long-term objectives beyond standard yearly mandate cycles and depending, of course, on what is more expedient and realistic in a specific environment. Mr. President, the UN has a proven positive track record of adapting its peace operations to different contexts And we should follow on, on that record, with increased flexibility. And by making progress achievable and more visible, we should find our way back to employing an underutilized instrument we all agree still provides one of the most cost-effective and legitimate approaches to conflict resolution. And my second point on process and follow-up concern is concerning the implementation of the Secretary-General's report. We would like to encourage the Secretariat to actively seek Member State support and commitment for the implementation of recommendations from the report, a framework which already has proved helpful and successful for the implementation of the Action for Peacekeeping initiative. Reforming and strengthening all peace operations must remain at the center of all our attention amongst Member States, in the Security Council, the General Assembly, and as part of the priorities of the next leadership of this organization. Germany remains committed to peacekeeping and will continue to contribute to these efforts, and we hope that together we can achieve real change and provide better solutions to those affected by crises we currently fail to address. Thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Germany for his statement. There are no more names inscribed on the list of speakers. The meeting is adjourned.
